assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work changed how economists and policymakers understand trade exposure, technology, local labour markets and wage inequality. It combines transparent identification with large, policy-relevant effects on employment, wages and adjustment, and it has spread well beyond labour economics.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock research is most clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's task and skill-premium work is also important, but it overlaps with earlier recognition of related work and with another list entry. The three-person group is the cleanest attribution, though it leaves out important co-authors outside this list.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from roughly 2013 to 2016, so more than a decade of replication, critique and extension is available. Later work on persistence and adjustment has refined the original findings.
uncertainties: Debate continues over the long-run size of the trade effects and how well the shift-share instruments identify them.
The prize could instead go to a broader technology-and-tasks group including Katz.
Authors outside the list may have strong claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory and empirics. The framework explains exporter behaviour, within-industry reallocation and gains from trade beyond the Krugman-style models, and it is now standard in research and in policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: The Melitz (2003) model is the central contribution. Helpman's work on firm-level trade, with Melitz and Yeaple, is closely linked and spans decades of trade theory. Redding is important for quantitative extensions, but his work is more derivative of the core model.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation and extension. The framework is embedded in the quantitative trade toolkit.
uncertainties: The committee may judge that a trade prize already went to Krugman in 2008.
Helpman is also credited under another trade entry, so a combined or alternative trade prize is possible.
The priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the dominant paradigm in the theory and practice of monetary policy. They underpin inflation targeting, policy rules and central-bank modelling, so the practical and conceptual impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: The list is large and diffuse. Calvo is credited with staggered pricing, Taylor with rules and staggered contracts, and Woodford with the integrated framework and its welfare analysis. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims for estimation and DSGE work. The three-name cap forces choices that are hard to defend.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use. Some recognition has already come through related prizes, such as Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Phelps and Bernanke.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested within a large group.
Post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experience raised questions about the framework's adequacy.
Calvo's age and prior recognition may matter.
Overlap with earlier macro prizes is a concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of demand and dynamic industry models made empirical industrial organisation quantitative. It supports merger analysis, antitrust and the evaluation of regulation. It is also used widely in trade, health and other fields.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP) are the standard credit for random-coefficients demand estimation. Pakes also has priority on dynamic games and entry (Ericson-Pakes, Pakes-McGuire). Bresnahan, Reiss and Benkard have real claims, but the three-name cap leaves them out.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1995 and has decades of practical use. Methodological refinements continue.
uncertainties: The committee must choose between the demand-estimation core and the dynamic-games line.
Bresnahan's claims may be seen as equal.
Structural assumptions are often hard to verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combining optimal-tax theory with empirical elasticities, notably for taxable income, gave a usable way to evaluate tax policy. It connects public-finance theory to administrative data and has shaped policy debate on top rates and tax enforcement.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod's work on taxable income and tax avoidance and Saez's sufficient-statistics and top-rate analysis are the core. Chetty and Stantcheva are important but younger, and Chetty has a separate claim under mobility research. Mirrlees and Diamond already received recognition for the theoretical foundations.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are from the late 1990s to 2010s and are confirmed by large literatures. Some estimates of the elasticity remain debated.
uncertainties: Estimates of the elasticity of taxable income are sensitive to identification and to the definition of income.
Saez also appears in an inequality entry, which could split support.
The prize may be seen as a continuation of earlier optimal-tax recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley built a theoretically grounded and empirically tested political economics. It covers electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal outcomes, and it links politics systematically to economic performance.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the closest pair through their joint books and papers on constitutions and policy. Besley's contributions on state capacity, accountability and development are separate but complementary. The group is plausible and coherent.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with work from the 1990s onward and a large following. A 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may reduce the perceived gap.
uncertainties: The 2024 institutions prize (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) may reduce the appetite for another prize in the area.
Causal identification of constitutional effects is often weak.
The group may be seen as less clearly distinct from the earlier laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine learning for causal inference, including debiased estimation and heterogeneous-effect methods, extended the credibility-revolution toolkit to high-dimensional data. It is influential in both academic and applied work.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov's double/debiased machine learning (with coauthors) and Athey's causal forests, with Wager, and policy-learning work are the main strands. Imbens has already been recognised for related work, and the group is young relative to other candidates. Attribution among coauthors is complicated.
assessment.maturity: The key work is from about 2016 to 2018 and is still developing. Adoption is rapid, but long-run durability is less settled than for older work.
uncertainties: It may be too early for a prize.
Credit is spread across many coauthors.
Athey also appears under digital markets, a second possible line.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance opened a large research agenda on how legal institutions, investor protection and ownership shape financial development and growth. It is among the most cited bodies of work in economics and finance and has influenced policy and cross-country research.
assessment.attribution: The core La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny papers are a tight group. Shleifer also has wider contributions in behavioural finance and corporate governance, so the four-name credit is stable but only three can be named.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are from the late 1990s. They have been widely tested and also criticised on both theory and measurement.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis faces serious empirical and conceptual criticism.
Cross-country regressions raise causality questions.
Shleifer's wider portfolio could shift the case to a different citation.
Vishny is left out by the three-name cap.
